whyCorrect: Pin down exactly what the conclusion claims before you read the choices: the amount of previous language exposure a dog has had may affect how well it tells a familiar language from an unfamiliar one. That is a claim about a relationship between two things, so the supporting finding has to vary both of them together. Age is the study's stand-in for amount of exposure, and telling familiar from unfamiliar means a gap between the brain's response to the accustomed language and its response to the other language. B is the only choice where that gap grows with age, which is exactly the more exposure, sharper discrimination pattern the team concluded.

whyWrong.A: This shows the dogs could tell the two languages apart, but it explicitly says dogs of all ages did so. Holding the effect constant across age removes any link to how much exposure a dog has had, so it supports half the conclusion and quietly undercuts the other half.
whyWrong.C: This compares the unfamiliar language with the scrambled recording, not the familiar language with the unfamiliar one. It speaks to whether dogs treat an unknown language as mere noise, which is a different claim from the one the team drew.
whyWrong.D: The comparison here is familiar language versus scrambled non-speech, so it measures the ability to distinguish speech from gibberish rather than one language from another. The age trend is the right shape but attached to the wrong contrast.

commonMistakes: Grabbing any choice that mentions age, or any choice that shows the dogs reacting differently to the two recordings, without checking that the choice pairs the age trend with the familiar-versus-unfamiliar comparison.
tips: In support-the-conclusion questions, write the conclusion as "more X goes with more Y" first; the correct finding must contain both X and Y, and the distractors usually swap one of them for something close by.

whyCorrect: The notes are about a 2019 seed-dispersal study in Oahu, and the two named plants matter because one is native and one is not, yet seeds of both turned up in the same place: the fecal samples of non-native birds. D is the only choice that puts both species together with that shared finding, which is what makes the researchers' conclusion about non-native birds dispersing native and non-native seeds land. Note that the stated goal sentence in this item talks about supercontinents, which nothing in the notes or the choices addresses, so the goal line does not belong to these notes.

whyWrong.A: It reports only that most Oahu plants are non-native and names a single non-native example, so it drops the native species entirely and says nothing about the birds or the seed dispersal the notes are built around.
whyWrong.B: It sets the two plants against each other by stressing that only one is native, emphasizing a difference rather than the shared fact that both showed up in the same fecal samples.
whyWrong.C: It restates the study's purpose and method without reporting what was found, so it uses the setup notes and skips the results that the named plants illustrate.

commonMistakes: Choosing the sentence that sounds the most like a study summary rather than the one that actually uses the specific details the goal asks you to feature.
tips: Read the goal sentence first and check it against the notes; if it names something the notes never mention, the item itself is broken, not your reading.

whyCorrect: Look at the sentence the two phrases sit in: "some studies emphasize the role of population density, others the role of average commuting distance, and so on, but walking decisions are made in complex contexts in which multiple conditions and needs inform individuals' choices." The phrases are there as examples of things research has already singled out as influential, and the "but" clause says each one is only a piece of a larger picture. That is precisely D: real influences, but only some among many.

whyWrong.A: The text never says these factors have been overemphasized. Alfonzo's complaint is that our overall understanding is not robust enough, not that any one factor has been given too much weight.
whyWrong.B: Nothing restricts these factors to Copenhagen. Copenhagen appears only as an example of a city whose features may not transfer, and the walkability research is discussed in general terms.
whyWrong.C: This flips the closing clause. The text says multiple conditions and needs do inform people's choices, not that people rarely consider these factors.

commonMistakes: Treating the word "insufficiently" as an attack on the individual factors; the text criticizes how incomplete the research picture is, not the factors themselves.
tips: For function questions, find the connector the phrases hang on. Here "but" tells you the examples are being framed as partial rather than wrong.

whyCorrect: The claim has two halves that the quotation must both satisfy: something new was developed in irrigation, and the result was greater efficiency. D supplies both in one sentence, since sprinkler systems are the innovation and the reduced share of water going to irrigation in the United States is the efficiency gain, made concrete by the contrast with the 70% figure worldwide. A quotation that only asserts efficiency would be desirable, or only describes an old design, leaves one half of the claim unsupported.

whyWrong.A: It compares humidity in two parts of California to explain where irrigation is needed. That is about geography and demand, not about any design change or any gain in efficiency.
whyWrong.B: It argues that improved efficiency would be valuable, which is a statement about why the goal matters. The student needs evidence that innovation has already delivered that improvement.
whyWrong.C: The point here is continuity, that a 7th-century design is still in use. Nothing says later innovation made irrigation more efficient, so it works against the claim more than for it.

commonMistakes: Picking B because the word "efficiency" appears in it; matching a keyword is not the same as supporting the claim built around it.
tips: Split the student's claim into its required parts and check each candidate quotation against every part before choosing.

whyCorrect: The passage is built on a contrast, and the second half is where Arnold speaks in his own voice. The Times reports the English ideal that everyone may do and look as he likes; Arnold answers that culture works tirelessly to move people toward a sense of what is truly beautiful, graceful, and becoming, and to make them like it. That second half is a statement about what culture does to people, so the text's purpose is to assert one of culture's principal effects.

whyWrong.A: Arnold's phrase "what is indeed beautiful" does imply a standard beyond personal preference, but he asserts it in passing rather than arguing for it. Nothing in the text sets out to establish that beauty is fact and not opinion.
whyWrong.B: The English appear only through the newspaper's defense of them, and Arnold treats that attitude as raw preference rather than analyzing any distinctive English taste.
whyWrong.C: The text says nothing about change over time. It contrasts two views held at the same moment, not an earlier view with a later one.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the first sentence and describing the newspaper's position as the text's purpose, when the sentence beginning "But culture" carries the author's actual point.
tips: In a main-purpose question with a "but" or "however" hinge, the author's claim almost always sits after the hinge.

whyCorrect: Compare the two cases the text puts side by side. Cuba is where the empire's legacy can still be heard, meaning Spanish is still spoken; Sardinia is a former imperial holding where Spanish is seldom spoken at all. The blank sits at the hinge between those opposite outcomes, so it needs a transition that signals a swing to the contrasting case, and "On the other hand" does exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Sometimes" only tells you how often the situation occurs. It leaves the relationship between the Cuba sentence and the Sardinia sentence unmarked, so the reversal the text is built on disappears.
whyWrong.C: "At the same time" points to two things holding simultaneously or to a qualification of the same case. The text is not qualifying what it said about Cuba; it is moving to a different colony with the opposite result.
whyWrong.D: "In addition" signals another item of the same kind. Sardinia is not more evidence that the empire's linguistic legacy survives, it is evidence that sometimes the legacy does not survive.

commonMistakes: Reading Sardinia as simply a second example of the empire's reach and reaching for an additive transition, when the point of the example is that Spanish did not stick there.
tips: Before choosing, state each side of the blank in five words. Here it is "Cuba still speaks Spanish" against "Sardinia barely does", and the opposition picks the transition for you.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a balance with two arms: warming could raise CO2 absorption by plants, and it could raise CO2 output from soil microorganisms. The researchers conclude that net CO2 rises when spring snow melts early, which can only happen if early melt pushes the output arm up, the absorption arm down, or both. A does both at once, since less soil moisture means the dogwood and other plants take up less CO2 while faster heterotrophic respiration releases more.

whyWrong.B: This is the opposite result. More absorption with unchanged respiration would drive net CO2 down, so it contradicts the conclusion rather than supporting it.
whyWrong.C: Plant growth slows, which cuts absorption, but respiration is suppressed, which cuts output too. With both arms falling, the finding cannot establish that the net balance rises.
whyWrong.D: Amplifying the effect of solar radiation on both plants and microbes leaves the two arms moving in the same direction by an unstated amount, so the net direction stays undetermined.

commonMistakes: Choosing any finding that mentions early snow melt affecting respiration without checking which way the plant side moves; net CO2 depends on the difference between the two, not on one of them.
tips: When a passage frames a question as a balance between two opposing processes, sketch an up or down arrow for each process in every choice and keep only the combination that forces the stated net result.

whyCorrect: The goal is to describe how the process cures an object, so the sentence has to name what does the curing and in what order it happens. The notes give a clear sequence: UV light images are projected up into a pool of liquid resin, the object hardens a layer at a time, and the finished object is baked to complete the curing. C reports that sequence accurately and keeps the two curing stages, light then oven, in the right order.

whyWrong.A: It makes the object itself pass through the dead zone and never mentions the UV light that actually cures the resin, so the mechanism the goal asks about is missing.
whyWrong.B: It says the curing is completed in the dead zone. The notes put the final curing in the oven; the dead zone is only the thin gap that lets oxygen and fresh resin flow in.
whyWrong.D: It has UV light solidifying layer by layer inside a dead zone that DLS creates, which garbles the notes. The resin is what solidifies, and it does so in the resin pool above the dead zone.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the choice that packs in the most technical vocabulary from the notes; a synthesis answer is judged on whether the details are used correctly, not on how many appear.
tips: For a how-does-it-work goal, check the order of stages in each choice against the numbered steps in the notes, and reject any choice that relocates a stage.

whyCorrect: Track what each sentence actually delivers. The first pair tells you when and where the Hispanic Society was founded and what it is devoted to; the last pair does the same for the Latino Cultural Center, ending on its focus on Latino cultures and art in the United States. The text is doing one job twice, introducing an institution and stating what it concentrates on, which is B.

whyWrong.A: Funding never comes up. The text says the Hispanic Society acquired more than 18,000 objects but never says how any purchase was paid for.
whyWrong.C: No historical development is traced. The two founding dates sit next to each other without any cause, trend, or event connecting them.
whyWrong.D: Only one collection size is given. With no figure for the Latino Cultural Center, there is nothing to contrast, and the passage never sets the two collections against each other.

commonMistakes: Letting the phrase "More recently founded" suggest a historical narrative; it is only a time marker distinguishing the second institution, not the start of a story about change.
tips: For a main-purpose question, summarize each sentence in a few words first. If your summaries repeat the same move, the purpose is that move, not something one sentence hints at.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the expectation: debris orbiting outside the Roche limit should clump together into a moon rather than stay a ring. Morgado's team found a ring at 2,500 miles when the limit is 1,100 miles, and it has remained intact, so the observation breaks the rule that was just stated. The blank needs a concessive transition marking that clash, and "though" is the only one that does.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" claims the finding matches what came before. It does the reverse, since a ring surviving outside the Roche limit is not what the stated principle predicts.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make Quaoar's ring an illustration of the rule. It is a counterexample, so labeling it an instance of the rule misreads the numbers.
whyWrong.C: "Fittingly" says the result is just what one would expect. The text stresses that the ring sits well outside the limit and is still intact, which is precisely the unexpected part.

commonMistakes: Skimming past the two distances and assuming any detected ring confirms the ring-forming rule; the whole point is which side of the 1,100-mile limit the 2,500-mile orbit falls on.
tips: When a transition sits between a stated rule and an observation, compare the numbers before choosing. The relationship is contrast whenever the observation lands on the wrong side of the rule's threshold.

whyCorrect: The passage defines an ekphrastic poem, then supplies two illustrations of the same thing. Alexander's poem meditates on an Alston painting; Eady's poem takes a Lawrence painting as its subject. Because the second case repeats the pattern of the first rather than altering it, the blank calls for a transition of similarity, and "likewise" is the one that says here is another instance of the same kind.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" signals that what follows holds despite what came before. Nothing about Alexander's poem creates an obstacle for Eady's; the two sit comfortably together.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" announces an opposite case. Both poems do exactly the same thing, take a painting as their subject, so there is no reversal to mark.
whyWrong.D: "Hence" claims the second poem is a consequence of the first. Eady's 2001 poem does not result from Alexander's 2011 poem, and the text draws no causal link between them.

commonMistakes: Assuming that a second example must contrast with the first, and reaching for "conversely" whenever two different names appear on either side of a blank.
tips: Ask what job the sentence after the blank is doing. If it repeats the job of the sentence before, the transition is additive or comparative, never contrastive.

whyCorrect: The passage turns on the word "But". First comes the newspaper's report of the English ideal, that everyone should be free to do and look just as he likes. Then Arnold gives his own point: culture works without rest to pull people toward a sense of what is truly beautiful, graceful, and becoming, and to make them like it. Describing what culture does to the people it reaches is a claim about one of culture's principal effects, which is A.

whyWrong.B: Arnold's phrase "what is indeed beautiful" leans on a standard beyond individual liking, but he never sets out to establish that beauty is objective. He assumes it while making a different point about what culture accomplishes.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text tracks change over time. It juxtaposes two positions held at the same moment, the newspaper's and Arnold's.
whyWrong.D: The English appear only as the subject of the newspaper's defense. No other group's taste is described, so no difference between groups is explained.

commonMistakes: Summarizing the first sentence, which reports the newspaper's view, instead of the sentence after "But", which carries the author's actual claim.
tips: In a short main-purpose passage with a contrastive hinge, the author's position is almost always the half that follows the hinge.

whyCorrect: The claim is narrow: Aristophanes mocks sophists for an inflated view of their own wisdom. So the quotation has to show a sophist praising himself, not an outsider complaining about sophists. In A, Socrates tells a paying newcomer to be ready for the moment he propounds "any clever dogma about abstruse matters", calling his own pronouncements clever and his own subjects deep in the same breath. That self-congratulation is the exaggerated wisdom the claim describes.

whyWrong.B: Strepsiades is an outsider describing what sophists teach, and his complaint is about absurd doctrines and about winning arguments right or wrong. That paints them as dishonest and ridiculous, not as vain about their own wisdom.
whyWrong.C: Socrates only asks whether the customer has a natural gift for speaking. He is sizing up the customer and says nothing at all about himself.
whyWrong.D: Strepsiades is urging his son to go and study. This shows a customer's enthusiasm for sophists, which is the reverse of a sophist's opinion of himself.

commonMistakes: Picking the longest, most obviously mocking quotation; B satirizes sophists, but the claim specifies the target of the satire, and evidence questions are decided by that specific wording.
tips: Underline the exact quality named in the claim, here an exaggerated sense of one's own wisdom, and require the quotation to show that quality coming from the person it is attributed to.
